idea.text: When metal compounds are heated in a hot flame, their electrons jump up to higher energy levels, then fall back and give out light. Each metal gives out its own colours, so the flame colour tells you which metal is there.
idea.analogy: Like a glowing fingerprint: every metal ion signs the flame with its own colour.

steps.title: Goggles on
steps.instruction: Goggles on, long hair tied back.

steps.title: Open the air hole
steps.instruction: Open the Bunsen's air hole so you get a hot, nearly invisible blue flame.

explore.then: You get a yellow, sooty, cooler flame. Its own yellow would hide the metal colours, especially sodium's.

steps.title: Light the Bunsen
steps.instruction: Turn on the gas and light the burner.

whatIf.order: Lighting a burner before goggles are on puts a flame and hot acid near unprotected eyes. Goggles first, always.

explore.if: turn the gas on and wait before lighting
explore.then: Gas builds up around the burner and lights with a whoosh. Have the flame ready, then turn on the gas.

steps.title: Clean the loop
steps.instruction: Dip the loop in the acid, then hold it in the flame until it adds no colour.

whatIf.order: There's no flame yet, so the loop can't be cleaned. Light the burner first.

explore.then: Leftover salt on the wire burns with its own colour, so you'd see a mix of colours and couldn't tell which metal you were testing.

steps.title: Test lithium
steps.instruction: Dip the clean loop in lithium chloride and hold it in the edge of the flame.

whatIf.order: Clean the loop first. Any leftover salt would colour the flame as well and confuse the result.

explore.if: hold the loop in the middle of the flame
explore.then: Just above the blue cone is the hottest part of the flame and gives the brightest colour. The middle is cooler.

steps.title: Clean again
steps.instruction: Clean the loop in acid and flame before the next metal.

whatIf.order: Test the current metal first, then clean the loop before the next one.

explore.then: Lithium left on the wire would add crimson to the next flame, so sodium's colour would look wrong.

whatIf.order: Clean the loop first. Leftover lithium would add crimson to the flame.

explore.if: test sodium and potassium mixed together
explore.then: Sodium's bright yellow swamps potassium's faint lilac. You'd only see yellow, unless you looked through blue cobalt glass.

steps.title: Clean again
steps.instruction: Sodium's yellow hides other colours. Clean thoroughly.

whatIf.order: Test the current metal first, then clean the loop before the next one.

explore.then: Even a trace of sodium gives a strong yellow that would hide potassium's lilac completely.

whatIf.order: Clean the loop first. Sodium is the worst for hiding other colours.

explore.then: The glass blocks yellow light, so any sodium contamination disappears and potassium's lilac shows clearly.

whatIf.order: Test the current metal first, then clean the loop before the next one.
Clean the loop first, so only calcium colours the flame.
Test the current metal first, then clean the loop before the next one.
Clean the loop first, so only copper colours the flame.

explore.if: use copper sulfate instead of copper chloride
explore.then: Still blue-green: the colour comes from the copper ion, not from the chloride or sulfate.

observations.whatHappened: Lithium gave a crimson flame, sodium an intense yellow-orange, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper blue-green.
observations.why: The flame's heat lifts electrons in the metal ions to higher energy levels. When they fall back they give out light of exact energies, and so exact colours, which are different for every element.

prompts.question: Which metal ion gave a lilac flame?
prompts.explain: Potassium gives lilac; it is easily hidden by sodium's yellow.

prompts.question: Why clean the loop between tests?
choices: Leftover salt would colour the next flame
prompts.explain: Traces of the last metal, especially sodium, would mask the next colour.

captions.text: Open the air hole and light the Bunsen: a hot blue flame.
captions.why: A blue flame (air hole open) is very hot and has almost no colour of its own, so any colour you see comes from the metal.
captions.safety: Hot flame and acid on the bench: goggles on and long hair tied back.

captions.text: Clean the loop in acid until the flame shows no colour.
captions.why: Acid dissolves leftover salt from the wire. Anything left on it would add its colour to the next metal's.
Lithium's electrons fall back across energy gaps that match red light.
Sodium's yellow is so bright that a tiny trace can hide other colours. That's why the loop is cleaned between tests.
Lilac is faint and easily hidden by sodium's yellow. Chemists sometimes look through blue cobalt glass, which blocks the yellow.
Different metals have different energy gaps, so they give different colours. Fireworks use these same metal salts for their colours.
